report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is too broad. Current evidence does **not** establish that simply following a vegetarian diet increases life expectancy versus eating meat. Evidence is observational (not long randomized lifespan trials), so diet is intertwined with smoking, alcohol use, body weight, exercise, socioeconomic factors, and—critically—the quality and amount of meat and plant foods eaten.

- A systematic review/meta-analysis found vegetarian diets were associated with lower *ischemic-heart-disease* mortality, but **no effect on all-cause mortality**; the authors rated the evidence low certainty. Thus it does not demonstrate longer overall life. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/
- In two British cohorts designed to include health-conscious meat eaters as comparators, overall mortality was essentially identical: vegetarian-to-nonvegetarian death-rate ratios were 1.01 and 1.03 (confidence intervals included no difference). https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/public-health-nutrition/article/mortality-in-british-vegetarians/F60895E8534D962978300E96B2E436F7
- Conversely, the Adventist Health Study-2 found lower all-cause mortality among vegetarian patterns. This supports a possible benefit, but Adventists are a distinctive, generally health-conscious population, limiting direct causal/general-population inference. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23836264/
- Meat is not one exposure: processed meat has stronger adverse evidence (including cancer hazard) than unprocessed meat, so “eating meat” is an overly crude comparison. https://publications.iarc.who.int/Book-And-Report-Series/Iarc-Monographs-On-The-Identification-Of-Carcinogenic-Hazards-To-Humans/Red-Meat-And-Processed-Meat-2018

A better-supported conclusion is that **well-planned, high-quality plant-forward diets can improve cardiovascular risk and may support longevity**, especially when they replace processed meat and refined foods—not that vegetarianism itself reliably lengthens life.
